heading: Language, data and who decides
intro: Machines learn from data, and some of the most careful training data in Canada is being gathered by Indigenous language speakers and communities. These connections show nêhiyaw (Cree), Tsuut'ina and Inuit language technology projects that train machines on recorded speech and text, and First Nations and Inuit principles about who owns and controls data. Each claim has a source.

connections.title: Teaching a computer to speak nêhiyawêwin
connections.text: At the University of Alberta in Edmonton, the Alberta Language Technology Lab (ALTLab) builds tools for Plains Cree with Cree speaking communities in Alberta. Its online dictionary, itwêwina, plays Cree words "graciously provided by the individuals from Maskwacîs," recorded with what is now the Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission. In 2019, ALTLab researchers trained a Plains Cree speech synthesizer on about 2.5 hours of Psalms read by Cree speaker Dolores Sand. At first the software lined up only 24 minutes of the audio with its text, and the voice was judged "unintelligible." After the team lined up all of it by hand, a former Cree language teacher called it "serviceable."

sources.title: Source of the 2.5 hour training set, the 24 aligned minutes and the listener judgments ("unintelligible", "serviceable"): Harrigan, Arppe and Mills, A Preliminary Plains Cree Speech Synthesizer, ComputEL 2019 (Association for Computational Linguistics)

Source of the Maskwacîs recordings quote and partners: itwêwina Plains Cree Dictionary, About (Alberta Language Technology Lab; Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission; speech synthesis based on recordings of Dolores Greyeyes Sand)

ALTLab, University of Alberta: 21st Century Tools for Indigenous Languages (Plains Cree as the spearhead language; works with Cree speaking communities in Alberta and Miyo Wahkohtowin Education, Maskwacîs)

connections.title: Tsuut'ina recordings for speech recognition
connections.text: Tsuut'ina Nation, a signatory of Treaty 7, is located in the southwest of Calgary. For a National Research Council Canada project working toward automatic speech recognition in Indigenous languages, Tsuut'ina Elder Bruce Starlight and Christopher Cox of Carleton University collected 25 to 30 hours of studio quality Tsuut'ina audio. The project says the recordings are to be distributed to Tsuut'ina Nation citizens and archived with the Nation's museum for long term preservation. CBC says Starlight served as the Nation's language commissioner and "has dedicated much of his life to language preservation." A speech recognizer can only learn the words and voices that are in its recordings.

sources.title: Source of the 25 to 30 hours recorded by Bruce Starlight and Christopher Cox, and their distribution to Tsuut'ina Nation citizens and the museum: National Research Council Canada, Toward automatic speech recognition in audio recordings of Indigenous languages
Source of the Nation's location and Treaty 7: Tsuut'ina Nation, Our History
Source of Bruce Starlight's role as language commissioner: CBC Radio, Unreserved, First words: Bruce Starlight speaks Tsuut'ina

connections.title: Inuktut and English, sentence by sentence
connections.text: Inuktut is an official language of Nunavut. Researchers at National Research Council Canada used the record of debates in Nunavut's Legislative Assembly, from 1999 to 2017, to line up about 1.3 million Inuktitut and English sentence pairs for machine translation. Language experts at Pirurvik, "an Inuit-owned institute of Inuktut higher learning" in Iqaluit, lined up around 8,500 sentence pairs by hand as a "gold standard" to check and improve the automatic matching. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami's National Inuit Strategy on Research names a priority to "Ensure Inuit access, ownership, and control over data and information."

sources.title: Source of Pirurvik's 8,500 hand aligned sentence pairs ("gold standard") and the Inuktut and English machine translation goal: National Research Council Canada, Project to create Inuktut language software and perform new text alignment for the Nunavut Legislative Assembly

Source of the 1.3 million sentence pairs (April 1999 to June 2017) and machine translation experiments: Joanis et al., The Nunavut Hansard Inuktitut-English Parallel Corpus 3.0 with Preliminary Machine Translation Results, LREC 2020
Source of the quote describing Pirurvik: Pirurvik Centre, About us (Inuit-owned institute of Inuktut higher learning, based in Iqaluit)
Source of the data priority quote: Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, news release on the National Inuit Strategy on Research (March 22, 2018)

connections.title: OCAP®: who owns and controls the data
connections.text: The First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC) sets out the First Nations principles of OCAP®: Ownership, Control, Access and Possession. Ownership "refers to the relationship of First Nations to their cultural knowledge, data, and information." Control means First Nations can seek control over research and information management that affects them. Possession "refers to the physical control of data." FNIGC calls OCAP® "a tool to support strong information governance on the path to First Nations data sovereignty." In this lab, a model learns only from the data it is given. OCAP® asks who should own and decide about that data first.

sources.title: Source of the OCAP® definitions and the data sovereignty quote: First Nations Information Governance Centre, Understanding OCAP® (OCAP® is a registered trademark of FNIGC)

try: The Plains Cree speech synthesizer was trained on about 2.5 hours of recordings, but at first the computer matched only 24 minutes of audio to the right words. Use Lesson 4 (More data, better data, new data) and the wrong labels slider in its learning curve model: was the first voice's problem mostly the amount of data or the quality of the data? Why did lining up the recordings by hand help so much?

Pirurvik's experts lined up 8,500 Inuktut and English sentence pairs by hand as a gold standard for checking the machine. In Investigation 2 (Train and test a bird call sorter), you test a model on examples it has not seen. Why should the checking examples be made by fluent speakers? Then use Lesson 5 and Investigation 3 (Narrow or general: task test): is an Inuktut to English translator narrow AI or general AI?

Tsuut'ina recordings go back to Tsuut'ina Nation citizens, ITK asks for Inuit access, ownership and control over data, and FNIGC sets out OCAP®. Lesson 4 says a machine learns only what its data shows it. Before anyone uses a community's language recordings to train AI, what questions should be asked, and who should get to answer them?

slide.title: Language, data and who decides
points: Edmonton: ALTLab trained a Plains Cree voice on 2.5 hours of speech, and fixing the data made it understandable.
Alberta: Tsuut'ina Elder Bruce Starlight helped record 25 to 30 hours of Tsuut'ina for speech recognition.
Canada: Inuit experts checked Inuktut translation data, and OCAP® and ITK say who should control data.
slide.notes: Use with Lesson 3 (Machine learning is trained from data) and Lesson 4 (More data, better data, new data), especially the wrong labels slider: the Cree synthesizer improved when its training data was lined up correctly by hand. Pair Pirurvik's hand checked sentence pairs with Investigation 2 (Train and test a bird call sorter). Use the Inuktut translator and Tsuut'ina speech recognition in Lesson 5 and Investigation 3 (Narrow or general: task test). Close with the data ownership question. Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing content: the lab and deck have no Indigenous content apart from the footer line "Edmonton, Treaty 6 territory", which needs no source. The voice recognition, voice typing and Chinook and Amii examples make no claim about any people. The deck's Lesson 4 notes say a voice system trained mostly on one group may work worse for others; the Tsuut'ina and Cree connections fit there, but I did not change that note.

Edmonton fit: ALTLab is at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, but the recordings came from Maskwacîs speakers and the synthesizer voice is Dolores Sand of Maskêko-sâkahikanihk, Saskatchewan (itwêwina names her Dolores Greyeyes Sand; the 2019 paper says Dolores Sand). Is a University of Alberta lab with Maskwacîs partners local enough for the Edmonton slot? I did not call Maskwacîs a Treaty 6 community because no page I fetched said so. The 2019 synthesizer is an older, preliminary system (built with Hidden Markov Models, not today's neural networks); I described it only as trained on recordings. Please also confirm the wording "what is now the Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission" (itwêwina says Miyo Wahkohtowin Education, now MESC).

Science framing: the Cree connection uses "lined up" for the paper's "aligned." I treat misaligned audio as a data quality problem, like wrong labels in Lesson 4. That is my link, not the paper's words. The last sentence of the Tsuut'ina text (a recognizer learns only the words and voices in its recordings) and the last two sentences of the OCAP® text are my own teaching links; FNIGC's page does not mention AI. Please confirm you are comfortable with them.

Tsuut'ina: the NRC page spells the museum "Tssu'tina Museum"; I wrote "the Nation's museum" to avoid repeating a possible misspelling. The NRC page does not say the speech recognizer is finished, so I wrote "working toward." CBC (2019) also says Starlight is "one of 29 remaining Tsuut'ina speakers"; I left that out as deficit framing and because the number may be out of date. I used a past tense "served" for his language commissioner role because CBC does. Would you like to contact Tsuut'ina Nation (for example its language department) to confirm Elder Starlight is comfortable being named in a school resource?

Inuktut and Inuktitut: NRC and Pirurvik write Inuktut; the corpus paper writes Inuktitut. I used Inuktut except for the corpus itself. I did not say the Hansard is published in both languages; I said the debates record was used for sentence pairs. The NRC page names no Inuit organization other than Pirurvik and does not describe how the Hansard data is governed, so I did not claim Inuit control of this project. The ITK quote sits beside it as Inuit's stated priority, not as a description of the project. Please check that this pairing reads fairly and not as criticism of Pirurvik or NRC.

OCAP®: OCAP® is a registered trademark of FNIGC and I kept the ® symbol. FNIGC offers OCAP® training; you may want to point teachers there rather than paraphrase further. OCAP® is First Nations principles; I did not apply it to Inuit or Métis, and I named ITK separately for Inuit.

Not used: the NRC Indigenous languages fact sheet says it offers texting suggestions in Plains Cree, but the NRC project page I fetched only lists Plains Cree keyboard layouts and gives predictive text for SENĆOŦEN, so I left predictive text out. The Michif recordings (Prairie to Woodland Indigenous Language Revitalization Circle) are not clearly tied to Alberta on the page, so I left them out; a Métis Nation of Alberta source on Michif technology would be a good addition. A 2022 ACL paper on low resource speech synthesis would not load, so I did not cite it. A 2009 University of Alberta Tsuut'ina news story used extinction framing, so I did not use it. I did not fetch the Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence position paper (Jason Edward Lewis et al.), so it is not cited; it could be a strong Indigenous authored source on AI if you want a fifth connection.

Knowledge Keeper: would you like to invite a nêhiyawêwin speaker through the Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission or ALTLab, or someone from Pirurvik, to talk with students about language and technology? I can add their own published words, with permission, in a later revision.

Across the three computer science labs: the itwêwina Plains Cree dictionary (University of Alberta ALTLab with Maskwacîs speakers) also appears in the Design Process Studio Lab (user-centred design) and the Programs and Instructions Lab (typing and searching in Cree syllabics), each time for a different idea. If that feels repetitive for a class doing all three, tell me which lab should keep it and I will find a different connection for the others.
